contentBlocks.body:
**Objective.** Make the API create, read, edit and delete actual rows with a clear resource contract.

This is a real project lab in projects/inventory-desk, also available from the Projects page as a source download. Work in an isolated copy of the reference project so you can compare your change with a known baseline. Read InventoryDesk.Api/Program.cs; InventoryDesk.Api/Domain.cs before editing. Trace one request from the UI or test through the boundary that owns the behavior.

**Acceptance criteria.** POST returns 201 and a Location header, GET reads the created values, PUT increments version, DELETE returns 204, and a later GET returns 404.

**Make a meaningful variation.** Add a product description field through an additive migration and a DTO update. Verify old rows receive a safe default. Write the observable expectation before editing the implementation. If the variation exposes a defect, keep the smallest failing fixture as a regression test.
Review rubric: HTTP verbs and status codes match the operation; ownership is not accepted from a request body; DTOs avoid exposing internal password or owner data.

**Explain the boundary.** Why return a DTO rather than serializing every entity field? Describe both a successful case and a rejected or missing-data case. Compare actual output with the acceptance criteria, including status codes, persisted values, and user-visible feedback where relevant.

**Evidence to keep.** Save the focused test result, a short before/after diff, and a note explaining one tradeoff. Completing the quiz records this lesson's concepts; it does not run the companion checks or certify that the project milestone is finished.

knowledgeItems.prompt: Why return a DTO rather than serializing every entity field?

choices: The public contract should expose only intentional fields
DTOs remove the need for validation
They make database writes automatically atomic
payload.answer: The public contract should expose only intentional fields
